meta.title: Who really said "Follow your bliss"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Joseph Campbell really said it — but not in any book he finished. It reached print in a 1971 interview and became famous through The Power of Myth in 1988.
meta.ogDescription: Yes — Joseph Campbell, on the record in The Power of Myth (1988). But the popular "universe will open doors where there were only walls" version is not his.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1904–1987 · American mythologist & professor at Sarah Lawrence College
answer.sourceLine: Campbell’s own maxim, spoken to Bill Moyers on camera and printed in the companion volume The Power of Myth (Doubleday, 1988): “My general formula for my students is ‘Follow your bliss.’” (p. 148). The Joseph Campbell Foundation notes it appears in none of the books he completed in his lifetime — it lived in his classroom and his interviews first, reaching print in a July 1971 Psychology Today conversation.

source.excerpt: … if you do follow your bliss you put yourself on a kind of track that has been there all the while, waiting for you, and the life that you ought to be living is the one you are living. … I say, follow your bliss and don’t be afraid, and doors will open where you didn’t know they were going to be.
trail: July 1971 — it reaches print. The Joseph Campbell Foundation states that the expression “does not occur in any of the books Campbell completed during his lifetime” and that its first appearance in print is an interview for Psychology Today ↗. The bibliography of Campbell’s work catalogues that interview as Sam Keen, “Man and Myth: A Conversation with Joseph Campbell,” Psychology Today 5 (July 1971): 35–39, 86–95 (OPUS Archives ↗).

1987–88 — it goes public. Campbell died on 30 October 1987. The six conversations he had recorded with Bill Moyers in his last summers aired on PBS from 21 to 26 June 1988 ↗, and Doubleday published the companion book, edited by Betty Sue Flowers, the same year.
The line itself. Wikiquote files the bare imperative Follow your bliss. in its sourced ‘The Power of Myth’ (1988) section ↗, citing Episode 1, Chapter 15 — not in the page’s disputed material.

Afterwards. The three words became a catchphrase within months of the broadcast. When students read it as licence for hedonism, Campbell is reported to have grumbled ↗, “I should have said, ‘Follow your blisters.’” — a remark sourced to a 2014 newspaper column, not to any Campbell text or tape.
source.excerptNote: Campbell’s answer when Bill Moyers asked whether he ever felt helped by hidden hands. Elsewhere in the same book he states the maxim flatly — “My general formula for my students is ‘Follow your bliss.’” (p. 148) — and traces the word to the Sanskrit sat-chit-ananda: being, consciousness, bliss.

author.name: Joseph Campbell
author.heading: Joseph Campbell
author.metaLine: 1904–1987 · American mythologist, writer, and professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College
author.bio: Campbell taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College from 1934 to 1972, building a comparative mythology that ran from Indigenous North America to the Upanishads and out again into Star Wars. His The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) gave storytellers the vocabulary of the hero’s journey, but the line most people know him by never made it into a book he finished. He died in October 1987, months before the six Bill Moyers conversations that turned “follow your bliss” into a national catchphrase reached television.

misattribution.heading: What gets bolted on
misattribution.intro: The three words are genuinely Campbell’s. Most of what travels alongside them is not.

items.who: “Follow your bliss and the universe will open doors for you where there were only walls.”
items.why: The most-shared long form of the line. Goodreads carries it credited to Campbell with no source at all ↗, above its own warning that quotes there are added by users and not verified. The sentence Campbell actually spoke, in the passage the Foundation reproduces from The Power of Myth, is “I say, follow your bliss and don’t be afraid, and doors will open where you didn’t know they were going to be.” No universe, no walls.

Passed around as Campbell’s own late-life correction, and it fits his temperament — but it is reported, not recorded. Wikipedia deliberately hedges that he “is reported to have grumbled” it ↗, citing a 2014 Napa Valley Register column rather than any Campbell manuscript, book or tape. Anecdote, not citation.

Campbell took the word from the Sanskrit sat-chit-ananda — being, consciousness, bliss — and drew the opposite line himself: “If your bliss is just your fun and your excitement, you’re on the wrong track” ↗ (The Hero’s Journey, p. 253). He was pointing at a deep vocation, not an indulgence.

misattribution.truthLine: Campbell said it, repeatedly and on the record — “My general formula for my students is ‘Follow your bliss’” ↗, The Power of Myth, p. 148. It is the greeting-card sentences bolted onto it that he never wrote.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: It started as classroom advice. Campbell taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College from 1934 to 1972, and the phrase was what he told students torn between the thing that lit them up and the thing their fathers wanted — “this one wants to study art, this one poetry, this one anthropology. But Dad says study law; that’s where the money is.” He never published it as a slogan. The Joseph Campbell Foundation is blunt about this: the expression appears in none of the books he completed during his lifetime.

Then it escaped. Campbell died on 30 October 1987, and the six conversations he had recorded with Bill Moyers aired on PBS the following June. Within months the three words were on posters, in commencement speeches and in self-help paperbacks — usually detached from the Sanskrit theology behind them and from the caveat Campbell attached when a young man asked whether he could be a writer: “Can you endure ten years of disappointment with nobody responding to you?”
detailsBody: Campbell explained the choice of word directly. In Sanskrit, he said, three terms mark “the brink, the jumping-off place to the ocean of transcendence”: sat (being), chit (consciousness), ananda (bliss or rapture). He could not be sure his consciousness was proper consciousness, or his being proper being — but he knew where his rapture was, so he held on to rapture and trusted it to deliver the other two. “I think it worked.”

That is why the Foundation’s own page pushes back on the hedonistic reading, quoting Campbell’s distinction from the 1971 Psychology Today interview: watch yourself and find “the real deep bliss — not the quick little excitement, but the real, deep, life-filling bliss.”

sourcesVerified.claim: The Joseph Campbell Foundation states the expression 'does not occur in any of the books Campbell completed during his lifetime' and that its first appearance in print is an interview for Psychology Today; the page also carries the Power of Myth p.120 exchange with Moyers ('doors will open where you didn't know they were going to be'), the p.148 line 'My general formula for my students is "Follow your bliss"', the sat-chit-ananda passage cited to The Power of Myth 120, the Hero's Journey p.253 warning 'If your bliss is just your fun and your excitement, you're on the wrong track', the 'not the quick little excitement, but the real, deep, life-filling bliss' quote cited to Psychology Today July 1971, the Thinking Allowed 1988 'Dad says study law' passage, and the 'ten years of disappointment' passage.

Wikiquote lists 'Follow your bliss.' in its sourced section for The Power of Myth (1988), cited to Episode 1, Chapter 15, and the full Moyers/Campbell 'hidden hands' exchange at p.120 in The Power of Myth (book) section. No bliss quotation appears in the page's Disputed section.

Wikipedia gives Campbell's dates as 26 March 1904 to 30 October 1987, American mythologist/writer/professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College 1934-1972; has a 'Follow your bliss' section with the sat-chit-ananda blockquote cited to Doubleday 1988 p.120; states he 'is reported to have grumbled, "I should have said, Follow your blisters"' citing Angela Hoxsey, Napa Valley Register, 5 December 2014; and lists Sam Keen, 'Man and Myth: A Conversation with Joseph Campbell', Psychology Today vol. 5 (1971), pp. 35-39, 86-95.

The PBS series aired 21-26 June 1988, after Campbell's death, from interviews recorded during the final two summers of his life; the companion book was published by Doubleday in 1988 with Betty Sue Flowers as editor.
The Joseph Campbell bibliography records: 'Man and Myth: A Conversation with Joseph Campbell. Sam Keen. Psychology Today 5 (July 1971): 35-39, 86-95.'
